title: Reviewing somebody else’s code: what to comment on and what to let go

videos.script: Bruno has opened a pull request. It lets customers choose a time to pick up their order, and he has asked you to review it. {{pr}} You open it, and you can see five things you would have done differently. {{five}} Here is the question this lesson is about. Which of the five do you say? {{question}} A review is not a test the author passes or fails. It is the moment a second person reads the change before customers meet it. Two people now understand this code instead of one, and a mistake has a second chance of being caught. {{purpose}} That only works if the comments are worth reading. Twenty remarks about spacing and one about a real bug look the same on the page, and the bug gets the same five seconds as the spacing. {{noise}} So you will learn an order for reading a change: what it is for, whether it works, whether somebody can understand it, and style last. {{order}} You will learn to write a comment that says how serious it is, why it matters, and what you would suggest. {{comment}} And you will learn what to let go. A preference is not a defect, and some of the most useful reviews say very little. {{title}}
